prompt: A random-pivot quicksort always returns the correct ordering, but the number of comparisons varies with its pivots. Which guarantee does this illustrate?

options.text: Deterministic: every run uses the same comparisons.

options.explanation: An expectation is not a limit on each execution.

options.text: Las Vegas: correct output with random running time.
options.explanation: Randomness affects work, not sorting correctness.

options.text: Monte Carlo: the output may be unsorted.
options.explanation: That is not the behaviour stated here.

workedExample: Separate correctness from resource use. Every permitted pivot sequence sorts, yet some sequences are much more expensive. That is the Las Vegas distinction.

prompt: A fixed composite number fools at most one-quarter of uniformly sampled Miller–Rabin bases. Why do fresh independent rounds improve the error bound?

options.text: A finite number of random rounds guarantees no error.
options.explanation: The upper bound can become tiny without becoming zero.

options.text: The composite must fool every independently sampled round.
options.explanation: The acceptance events combine multiplicatively under the stated model.

options.text: Repeating the same base creates the same reduction.
options.explanation: Reusing one outcome adds no independent chance of detecting compositeness.

options.text: The fixed-input bound becomes the posterior chance of compositeness.
options.explanation: That posterior also depends on candidate selection.

workedExample: Condition on the input being the same fixed composite. Rejection on any round reveals it; acceptance requires all rounds to be fooled. Independence is what supports multiplying the per-round bounds.
